rv.q: This history lesson also demonstrates the power of making humanity sing, even in our darkest hours.

The show is superbly sung throughout (it’s a real treat for fans of this genre), the numbers are rich and stylish and the story quite enveloping, especially given the familiarity of the genre of entertainment biographies.
With Manilow’s fine music, and this extraordinary company of actors, it’s worth the extra mileage.
Every time the production becomes a little wobbly, those songs steer it back to solid emotional ground.
The second half is where things go off-key, falling into cliché.
The Manilow-Sussman version is joyful and, in the end, profoundly moving, even as it risks crossing the line into shameless tear jerking.
It's a tale eminently worth telling, a moment of grace and good fellowship amid years of horror.
With minor exceptions, Harmony hits all the right notes.
Harmony, finally receiving its New York debut with the National Yiddish Theatre Folksbiene, has been in the musical theater ether since the late '90s when the show premiered at La Jolla Playhouse.
What’s most extraordinary about “Harmony,” though, is how little is in need of embellishment.
The startling and innovative outweighs the cliched in this tuneful and harrowing musical.

Manilow and Sussman’s work to keep their legacies alive is admirable, and what their musical lacks in out-of-the-boxness, it more than makes up through the classic art of telling an unsung story well.
Harmony proves to be an entertaining and absorbing show derivative of many earlier Broadway classics.

The show is handsomely staged by Warren Carlyle (choreographer of “The Music Man”) but extremely uneven, with generic pop ballads and comedy bits juxtaposed against historical exposition and downbeat drama.
Regardless of some unevenness in the book, Harmony is delightful and deeply moving.

Fans of Mr. Manilow may be disappointed if they are expecting his trademark modulating romantic pop songs from the seventies but will be pleasantly surprised by the deviation and the valid musical theater score he has composed.
The show is too long and some songs drag on.

This story about six Berlin-based performers finding fame and romance under the rise of Nazism is aided by a personable cast, clever choreography by Warren Carlyle, who also directs masterfully, and a handful of knockout songs.
Regardless of the obstacles it’s already overcome, though, it still lacks the creative propulsion such a leap would require.

cn.t: Critics find Manilow's long-gestating musical about the Comedian Harmonists mostly compelling, praising its tuneful score and timely story of a singing group destroyed by Nazis, though some cite uneven execution and melodramatic moments.
